# AI Catalyst — GitHub Copilot Instructions

GitHub Copilot Chat loads this file automatically for every session in this
repo. Its contents apply to all skills, all generated artifacts, and any
code authored or reviewed in this workspace. Claude Code users: skills in
this repo reference this file via relative links — follow it the same way
Copilot does.

This file covers two surfaces:

1. **Code authoring / chat** — corporate-network artifact registries
   (mandatory, see below).
2. **Code review** — how to cite the RFD 0008 coding standards in PR
   review comments.

---

## Internal artifact registries (mandatory)

**Public package repositories are blocked on the Capital Group corporate network** to mitigate supply-chain attacks against open-source registries. Every install command, Dockerfile `FROM`, package config file, and CI step — whether in this repo, in skill outputs, or in code generated by skills — **must** route through the internal Nexus mirrors below. This is a hard requirement, not a recommendation.

| Ecosystem | Internal URL |
|---|---|
| pip (PyPI) | `https://cgrepo-aws.capgroup.com/repository/cgpypi/simple/` *(also reachable as `https://cgrepo.capgroup.com/repository/cgpypi/simple/` — same Nexus, mirrored hostnames)* |
| conda | `https://cgrepo-aws.capgroup.com/repository/conda-proxy/` |
| npm | `https://cgrepo-aws.capgroup.com/repository/cgnpm/` |
| Maven (releases) | `https://cgrepo-aws.capgroup.com/repository/cgmaven/` |
| Maven (snapshots) | `https://cgrepo-aws.capgroup.com/repository/maven-snapshots/` |
| NuGet | `https://cgrepo-aws.capgroup.com/repository/cgnuget-v3/` |
| Docker | `cgregistry-aws.capgroup.com/<image>:<tag>` |

Authoritative source: [`cg-open-itg/harness-hub` → `docs/technical-documentation/artifacts-repository/artifacts-consuming-examples.md`](https://github.com/cg-open-itg/harness-hub/blob/main/docs/technical-documentation/artifacts-repository/artifacts-consuming-examples.md).

### Patterns to use in generated artifacts

- **`requirements.txt`** — first line: `--index-url https://cgrepo-aws.capgroup.com/repository/cgpypi/simple/`
- **`pip install` in shell/CI** — pass `--index-url https://cgrepo-aws.capgroup.com/repository/cgpypi/simple/` or rely on a configured `pip.conf`
- **`Dockerfile`** — `FROM cgregistry-aws.capgroup.com/python:3.11-slim` (never `FROM python:3.11-slim`)
- **`package.json` projects** — commit a `.npmrc` with `registry=https://cgrepo-aws.capgroup.com/repository/cgnpm/`
- **`pom.xml` / `build.gradle`** — declare the cgmaven repository (see harness-hub doc)
- **`.condarc`** — `channels: [https://cgrepo-aws.capgroup.com/repository/conda-proxy/]` with `default_channels: []`

### Diagnostic — how a missed re-pointing shows up

When something still points at a public registry, the corporate network block surfaces as **a 404 (or connection refused / connection timeout) against the public host** — not as a "package not found" error from the mirror. Signatures to watch for:

- `pypi.org` / `files.pythonhosted.org` → 404 or timeout in pip output
- `registry.npmjs.org` → 404 or `ETIMEDOUT` in npm output
- `registry-1.docker.io` / `auth.docker.io` → 404 or `dial tcp: i/o timeout` in `docker pull`
- `repo.maven.apache.org` / `repo1.maven.org` → 404 or timeout in `mvn`
- `repo.anaconda.com` → 404 in `conda install`

If you see one of these against a public host, the fix is **not** to find a different package — it's to re-point the tool at cgrepo. Confirm by greping the failing config (`pip.conf`, `.npmrc`, `Dockerfile`, `pom.xml`, `.condarc`, `requirements.txt`, CI workflow) for `cgrepo` and the corresponding host above.

## Code review — citing RFD 0008 standards

This repository follows the coding standards in [RFD 0008](../rfd/0008/README.md).
Every rule has a stable ID of the form `LANG-CATEGORY-NNN`. The full
machine-readable index is `rfd/0008/standards.yaml`.

### 1. Cite the rule ID in every suggestion

Format: `LANG-CATEGORY-NNN — short directive`

This lets the author navigate directly to the rule definition. Always
include a link to the rule in the per-language file.

**Good:**
> **PY-IDIOM-010** — `pathlib` only; never string concatenation or `os.path`.
> The path on line 47 is built with `+`, which is OS-fragile and breaks on
> filenames with special characters. Use `Path(base_dir) / filename`.
> ([rule](../rfd/0008/python/idiom.md#py-idiom-010))

**Bad:**
> Consider using pathlib here.

### 2. Verify the rule ID exists before citing

Before citing a rule, confirm it appears in `rfd/0008/standards.yaml`. Do
not invent rule IDs (`PY-NAMING-099`) that don't exist. If the issue you're
flagging doesn't have a corresponding rule, describe the issue in plain
language and don't fabricate an ID.

### 3. Prioritize by severity

Each rule has a severity in `standards.yaml`:

- **`error`** — flag every violation. These are correctness or governance
  issues; they block merges via CI when a linter exists.
- **`warning`** — flag if the rationale clearly applies to the changed
  code. Skip if the violation is in unchanged context.
- **`advisory`** — skip unless the violation is egregious. These are
  stylistic recommendations without linter enforcement.

### 4. Don't restate linter feedback

If a rule has a `linter` field with a code (e.g., `ruff:E722`,
`clippy:unwrap_used`, `sqlfluff:capitalisation.keywords`), CI already
catches it. Don't comment on the same violation Copilot would. Focus on
what linters can't catch:

- Unclear naming and intent
- Missing or weak tests for new business logic
- Missing documentation on new public surface
- Cross-cutting violations: a function that satisfies every individual
  rule but is structurally wrong
- Architectural smell: misplaced responsibilities, leaking abstractions,
  bad coupling
- Security implications of the specific change (not generic OWASP advice)

### 5. Read the rule body before flagging

Each rule has a Decision, Why, Exception, and Examples section in the
per-language file. Before flagging, check the Exception clause — many
rules have legitimate exceptions that may apply to the changed code.

### Per-language rule files

| Language / Platform | File | Categories |
|---|---|---|
| Python | `rfd/0008/python/` | VERSION, IMPORT, NAMING, TYPE, DOC, ERROR, IDIOM, TEST, SECURITY |
| Rust | `rfd/0008/rust/` | VERSION, IMPORT, NAMING, TYPE, ERROR, IDIOM, ASYNC, LOG, DOC, TEST, SECURITY, CARGO, PERF |
| Java | `rfd/0008/java/` | VERSION, IMPORT, NAMING, TYPE, NULL, ERROR, IDIOM, LOG, DOC, TEST, IMMUTABILITY, CONCURRENCY, SECURITY, SPARK |
| TypeScript | `rfd/0008/typescript/` | VERSION, IMPORT, NAMING, TYPE, REACT, IDIOM, ASYNC, ERROR, TEST, SECURITY |
| SQL / dbt | `rfd/0008/sql/` | VERSION, FMT, NAMING, CTE, MODEL, INCR, TEST, JINJA, IDIOM, PERF, SECURITY |
| Databricks / UC | `rfd/0008/databricks/` | DELTA, UC, COMPUTE, WORKFLOW, SEC |

Each language directory has a `README.md` with intro and tooling, plus
one file per category (e.g., `python/error.md` for `PY-ERROR-*`). To
locate a specific rule, look it up in `rfd/0008/standards.yaml` — the
`source` field gives the exact file and anchor.

### Review priorities (in order)

When reviewing a PR, focus attention in this order:

1. **Correctness over style.** A subtle bug beats a style nit. If you only
   have one comment to make, make it about correctness.
2. **Security findings.** Anything in the SECURITY / SEC categories or
   matching obvious vulnerability patterns (SQL injection, secret in code,
   missing input validation at API boundary).
3. **Missing tests for new business logic.** Specifically:
   - Python: `PY-TEST-005` (no `assert True`), new functions without tests
   - Rust: new public API without `#[test]` or `#[tokio::test]`
   - TypeScript: new component without React Testing Library tests
   - SQL: new business-logic model without `SQL-TEST-005` unit tests
4. **Missing documentation on public API.**
5. **Naming clarity.** Generic names (`data`, `result`, `temp`) on
   non-trivial variables; missing prefixes (`is_`, `_id`, `_at`).
6. **Architectural concerns.** Cross-cutting violations, misplaced
   responsibilities, abstractions that leak.

### What NOT to flag

- Issues already caught by CI linters (rule has a `linter` field)
- Pure style preferences not encoded in the standards
- Rules with `severity: advisory` unless egregious
- Code in files not changed by the PR (out of scope)
- Test fixtures or test files for rules that are exempted via
  `per-file-ignores` (see each language's tooling section)

### Rule ID examples by category

```
PY-NAMING-001       Python: identifier casing
PY-ERROR-001        Python: never bare except
PY-IDIOM-010        Python: pathlib only
PY-SECURITY-002     Python: parameterized SQL only

RS-ERROR-001        Rust: never .unwrap() outside tests
RS-ASYNC-005        Rust: never block the runtime
RS-SECURITY-001     Rust: unsafe denied at workspace

JV-NULL-002         Java: never Optional.get without isPresent
JV-TYPE-003         Java: switch expressions over switch statements
JV-IMMUTABILITY-002 Java: defensive copies of mutable parameters/returns

TS-TYPE-002         TypeScript: never any; use unknown
TS-REACT-009        TypeScript: TanStack Query for server state
TS-SECURITY-003     TypeScript: auth tokens in httpOnly cookies

SQL-MODEL-002       SQL: always ref() and source()
SQL-CTE-005         SQL: final CTE named `final`
SQL-IDIOM-005       SQL: never DISTINCT to fix duplicates

DBX-UC-001          Databricks: three-part names everywhere
DBX-UC-003          Databricks: external tables preferred over managed
DBX-SEC-002         Databricks: OAuth client credentials, never PAT
```

### When the rule doesn't fit

If you find a code smell that doesn't map to any rule in the standards,
describe the issue in plain language without fabricating a rule ID. End
the comment with: *"This may be worth proposing as a new rule in RFD
0008."* — that signals the gap to the standard's owner.

### Format reminder

Keep review comments concise. The shape that works:

```
**RULE-ID** — short directive.
One or two sentences explaining how the changed code violates the rule.
Concrete suggestion. ([rule](../rfd/0008/<file>.md#rule-id))
```

Avoid:

- Multi-paragraph explanations of well-known rules
- Restating the rule's full Decision/Why/Exception sections
- Suggesting the entire rule be applied to unchanged code
